claim.pdf_says: D.19.5.4   Polymorphism  /  D.19.5.4.1   General — D.19.5.4 printed at the same rank as D.19.5.1/.2/.3; D.19.5.4.1 one rank below it.
claim.markdown_says: ## D.19.5.4 Polymorphism (specs/ISO_COBOL.md:46274) and ### D.19.5.4.1 General (:46277) — D.19.5.4 at markdown level 2 while its sibling D.19.5.1 is at level 3, and the fifth-level D.19.5.4.1 lands at level 3 alongside it.
claim.why_it_matters: The fourth- and fifth-level clauses are both one to two levels too shallow, so D.19.5.4.1 General ends up at the same markdown depth as D.19.5.1 Inheritance even though the PDF prints them two ranks apart. The heading tree contradicts the printed numbering.

verdict.reasoning:
REFUTED on five independent grounds, verified against the 300 dpi render of PDF page 1149 (printed folio 1119) and against specs/ISO_COBOL.md.

(1) NOTHING IS MISSING — the 'missing-heading' label is false on its face. The PDF prints exactly two headings on this page: bold 'D.19.5.4   Polymorphism' and bold 'D.19.5.4.1   General'. The markdown carries both, verbatim, with the dotted numbers intact and in the correct order and position (line 46274 '## D.19.5.4 Polymorphism', line 46277 '### D.19.5.4.1 General'), each with a correct anchor (section-d-19-5-4, section-d-19-5-4-1). Not one character of heading text or numbering is absent, reordered, or altered. The body paragraph that follows ('Polymorphism is supported by COBOL in two different ways...') is also transcribed complete and correct.

(2) THE CLAIM MISQUOTES THE PDF. I cropped and enlarged the heading block (original px x=280-1500, y=2320-2620) and looked at the printed glyphs directly. 'D.19.5.4   Polymorphism' and 'D.19.5.4.1   General' are set in the SAME bold serif face, at the SAME point size, on the SAME left margin, with the SAME leading above and below. The PDF applies NO typographic rank distinction between them whatsoever. The claim's assertion that the PDF 'prints them two ranks apart' is not an observation of the page — it is inferred from the dotted number alone. Since the dotted number is exactly what the markdown preserves verbatim, the one and only rank signal the PDF actually carries is fully present in the transcription.

(3) THE CLAIM MISDESCRIBES THE MARKDOWN by cherry-picking one sibling. The four fourth-level siblings are: '### D.19.5.1 Inheritance' (:45936), '## D.19.5.2 Restricting inheritance...' (:46074), '## D.19.5.3 Conformance' (:46090), '## D.19.5.4 Polymorphism' (:46274). D.19.5.4 therefore AGREES with two of its three siblings at level 2; it is D.19.5.1 that is the odd one out. The claim selected the single non-matching sibling and framed D.19.5.4 as the anomaly, inverting the actual majority.

(4) NOT A PAGE-1149 DEFECT — markdown '#' depth does not encode numeric rank ANYWHERE in this transcription. Whole-file histogram: 947 '#', 2304 '##', 1413 '###', only 96 '####'. Four-component section numbers land on '###' and '##' interchangeably throughout the body of the standard: '### 5.2.6.1 General', '### 5.2.6.4 Choice indicators', '### 6.2.3.1 General' but '## 6.2.3.2 Syntax rules'; '### 7.2.4.2 General format', '### 7.2.4.3 Syntax rules' but '## 7.2.4.4 General rules'. The spec's numbering goes deeper than four components while the file effectively bottoms out at '####'. So the p1149 pattern is the transcription's document-wide (noisy) heading convention, not a discrepancy introduced on this page. Filing it per-page would generate hundreds to thousands of identical entries for a single global property.

(5) NO MEANING CHANGES. The authoritative hierarchy signal in an ISO document is the dotted clause number, and it is transcribed exactly. Any reader or tool recovers 'D.19.5.4.1 is a subclause of D.19.5.4 is a subclause of D.19.5 is a subclause of D.19' from the number itself. Normative content, syntax, general rules, and cross-reference targets are all unaffected. This falls squarely under the reject criteria 'the difference is only ... formatting' and 'the difference does not change meaning'.

The finding is a rendering-convention artifact of the markdown transcription, mislabeled as a missing heading and supported by a misdescription of both sources.
verdict.corrected_description: No discrepancy. Both headings the PDF prints on page 1149 — 'D.19.5.4   Polymorphism' and 'D.19.5.4.1   General' — are present in specs/ISO_COBOL.md at lines 46274 and 46277 with their text, dotted numbering, order, anchors and following body text all correct, so nothing is missing. The PDF itself sets the two headings in identical bold face, size and left margin with no typographic rank distinction at all, so the claim that the PDF 'prints them two ranks apart' misdescribes the page; the only rank signal the PDF carries is the dotted number, which the markdown reproduces verbatim. The claim also misdescribes the markdown by comparing D.19.5.4 only against '### D.19.5.1' while omitting that D.19.5.2 and D.19.5.3 are likewise '##' — D.19.5.4 matches the majority of its siblings. Finally, markdown '#' depth never encodes numeric rank in this transcription (four-component numbers appear as both '##' and '###' throughout, e.g. '### 5.2.6.1' vs '## 6.2.3.2' vs '## 7.2.4.4'; only 96 '####' in the entire file), so this is a document-wide formatting convention rather than a page-1149 defect. If the inconsistent heading depth is to be addressed at all, it belongs as a single global normalization task for the transcription pipeline, not as a structural per-page reconciliation finding.
